tierWindow.goal: Build a revision strategy: organise your time and your knowledge gaps into a plan, and populate it with active techniques chosen to fit your material.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and organisation (apply, build, select, plan), beyond the introductory understand/identify level and short of the advanced self-directed adaptation.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Structured multi-step tasks: assembling a strategy from parts, contrasting active with passive approaches, and matching techniques to material.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked examples contrast a weaker and a stronger approach; the learner makes choices and plans, with guidance.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already understands what exams are and why a revision strategy is needed (the introductory tier). They are now ready to put that into action: to build a strategy and choose techniques for it, rather than only recognising that one is necessary. They have not yet mastered the self-directed application of techniques or exam-day performance (the advanced tier).

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has four short lessons. First, the two building blocks of a revision strategy: your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge. Second, what makes revision active rather than passive. Third, matching technique families, visual, auditory and kinaesthetic, to your material. Fourth, bringing strategy, active technique and material together so you revise on purpose rather than by habit. Work through them in order; the last lesson depends on the first three.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the four lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about building a revision strategy rather than simply starting to revise. By the end you will be able to build a strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, apply active-learning principles so your revision tests you rather than just reminding you, and select technique families, visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, to match your material.

None of this assumes you already revise well. It assumes you want your revision time to do more than it currently does, and shows you how to connect the pieces so it does.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: build a strategy around time and knowledge gaps, apply active-learning principles instead of passive review, select technique families to fit the material.

practiceConnection.academic: Treating your own knowledge as something you can audit, rather than something you either have or do not, is a habit that extends well past exam revision. The same move, checking honestly where the gaps are before deciding what to do next, is worth applying to any piece of coursework or professional task you take on.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced revising and exams course turns an individual strategy into something you can sustain and adapt under real exam pressure across a whole module or year. Going wider: the same discipline of auditing what you know before deciding what to do next underpins Academic Writing, Researching and Reflective Practice.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Revision is no longer just something you start the week before an exam: you can build a strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, apply active-learning principles so your sessions test you rather than just remind you, and select the technique family that actually fits what you are revising. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, treating revision as a strategy built from parts that fit together, time, technique and material, rather than a single habit applied regardless, is one you can carry into any sustained piece of academic or professional preparation.
